tool.title: Black robin
tool.excerpt: The black robin or Chatham Island robin is an endangered bird from the Chatham Islands off the east coast of New Zealand. It is closely related to the South Island robin. It was first described by Walter Buller in 1872. The binomial commemorates the New Zealand botanist Henry Travers (1844–1928). Unlike its mainland counterparts, its flight capacity is somewhat reduced. Evolution in the absence of mammalian predators made it vulnerable to introduced species, such as cats and rats, and it became extinct on the main island of the Chatham group before 1871, being restricted to Little Mangere Island and Rangatira Island thereafter.

tool.excerpt: Black Robin, Once Down to Five Birds, Wins NZ Bird of the Year Tuesday, September 22, 2026 Headlines & Global News Subscribe World U.S. Business Tech Science/Health Sports Entertainment Trending Science/Health Science Black Robin, Once Down to Five Birds, Wins NZ Bird of the Year Every karure alive today descends from a single breeding pair, and its victory crowns one of the world’s most celebrated conservation recoveries. By Alan Simmons Published: Sep 22 2026, 4:44 AM EDT Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Reddit Share on Flipboard Share on Pocket FILE: A Chatham Islands black robin, or karure, wearing an identification band on its leg, perches on a branch in New Zealand's Chatham Islands on July 27, 2015. The critically threatened species, reduced to five birds in 1980, was voted New Zealand's 2026 Bird of the Year with a record 105,000 people casting ballots. Peter de Lange/Wikimedia Commons CC0 1.0 While much of the world spent the weekend counting ballots in rather weightier contests, New Zealanders turned out in record numbers for an election of their own — and handed victory to a small, entirely black songbird that 46 years ago was five individuals away from vanishing from the Earth. The karure, or Chatham Islands black robin, was crowned New Zealand's 2026 Bird of the Year on Monday, finishing atop the field with 26,610 votes, according to Forest & Bird, the independent conservation organization that runs the annual competition. The robin beat out two celebrated former champions — the kākāpō, the world's heaviest flightless parrot, which had led early voting, and the kārearea, New Zealand's native falcon — into second and third place. The turnout was itself a story. More than 105,000 people cast ballots, the most in the competition's two-decade history and roughly one in every 50 New Zealanders — up from about 75,000 last year and a world away from the fewer than 900 votes recorded in the contest's first edition.
